body:
In the end, constraint validation isn't supposed to be a perfect solution for script-less form validation. I think your best bet for more complicated use cases like this is going to involve writing a little JavaScript to encode your page's specific logic. The spec's `checkValidity`, `reportValidity`, and `setCustomValidity` functions give you the right building blocks for this. As you mention in your (2), this will be a bit more work. You can also do things like right before submit time, or before the "invalid" event fires, ignoring invalidity that arises from only one of the required fields being missing. But it's not a goal of this spec to support every scenario without scripting; I don't know what's "non-native" about script solutions, but script solutions are what this spec is giving you.

Hope that helps!

As you said the spec cannot support _every_ scenario, but it still gives a faster way to handle required input. Complex cases (such as form dependency) should be solved by the author, for sure, but what I pointed out as n.2 is a very easy use case.

In short, I'd strongly suggest extending to all controls the "alternative mechanism" used for radio buttons: two or more controls having the same name would share the same "missing value" flag and the form would be valid if at least one is checked/selected/filled in. For instance it would be useful for checkbox lists where at least one item must be selected, but it would also allow choices like the one in my example. Finally, a name ending with square brackets (e.g. `name="foo[]"`) would allow the server to process each submitted value in the list.

Additional work does not scare me. Sometimes I am a bit more concerned by internationalisation, so _custom validity functions_ would be just a little more troublesome (I would rather resort to handle "invalid" fields before submission).
